name: Gautama Swami
summary: Born Indrabhuti Gautama, he was a learned Brahmin who became the senior-most of Mahavira's eleven chief disciples. Jains remember him at Diwali and at the new year.
about: Jain tradition says Gautama Swami was born as Indrabhuti Gautama in the village of Gorbara in Magadha. A learned Brahmin, he came to challenge Mahavira in debate and was won over, becoming the senior-most of Mahavira's eleven ganadharas. Jain texts say these chief disciples remembered Mahavira's teaching and passed it on by word of mouth, which became the Agamas. Jains believe he attained omniscience right after Mahavira's liberation, a moment linked with Diwali and the start of the Jain new year. Svetambara Jains also invoke his name for good fortune in new account books.
kidSummary: Gautama Swami was the main student of Mahavira. Jain stories say he came as a proud scholar to argue with Mahavira, but ended up as his follower. Many Jain families remember him on the new year, hoping for a bright start.

story.title: A famous teacher
story.text: Indrabhuti Gautama was a respected scholar who taught many students and led religious ceremonies in his village.

story.title: A challenge
story.text: One account says he went to challenge Mahavira in debate, perhaps because he was angry that so many people were listening to someone else.

story.title: Changing his mind
story.text: Mahavira answered his doubts, and Gautama became his student. Ten other scholars followed him, and together they were the eleven chief disciples.

story.title: A tie of love
story.text: Gautama loved his teacher so much that this held him back from full knowledge. Mahavira sent him on an errand, and when he returned Mahavira had gone. After grieving, Gautama let go.

story.title: A new year of light
story.text: Jains believe Gautama attained full knowledge right after Mahavira's liberation, so Diwali and the new year are linked to him.

teaches: Questions and debate can lead to truth
Let go of attachment, even to a beloved teacher
emblems: Name written in new account books

facts.text: One account says Gautama gathered gods for a sacrifice, but the gods flew off to hear Mahavira preaching nearby.

A Jain teaching booklet says that all of Gautama's own disciples, and nine of the other ganadharas, had reached omniscience, but he had not. Mahavira told him his great affection for his guru was the obstacle, and that he must let even that go.
On the day Mahavira was to reach nirvana, he sent Gautama to a nearby village to teach a man named Devsharma. Gautama came back to find that his teacher had already gone.

Svetambara tradition says Gautama fed some 1,500 hermits rice pudding from one small bowl, keeping his thumb in it to call on a special power that stops food running out. This is why he is linked with plenty.

In a Svetambara story, 1,500 hermits failed to climb Mount Ashtapada, but Gautama succeeded in reaching it to honour the 24 Tirthankaras. Impressed, the hermits became his disciples and then Jain monks.

Svetambara texts record a meeting in the Tinduka park at Shravasti between Gautama and Keshi, a senior follower of the earlier Tirthankara Parshvanatha. Their followers wondered whose teaching was right, so the two sat down to talk before a crowd.
Keshi asked why Parshvanatha taught four vows while Mahavira taught five. Gautama said the people of each age needed a different form of the same goal. Keshi was convinced and adopted the five vows.
In the Kalpa Sutra, the night Mahavira died, eighteen allied kings (nine Mallakis and nine Lichchhavis) lit lamps, saying that since the light of knowledge was gone they would make a light of matter.
Svetambara Jains write his name in new account books at the new year as a sign of good luck.

Gautama once doubted a layman named Ananda, who claimed a rare clairvoyance. Mahavira said Ananda was right and told Gautama to apologise, so Gautama set aside his alms and went straight back to ask forgiveness.
The Bhagavati Sutra is the largest text of the Jain canon and is said to hold 36,000 questions answered by Mahavira. Its questioners include Gautama, who appears first in the list.
Uttaradhyayana chapter 10 repeats an urging to Gautama to stay alert all the while. It compares life to a fallen dry leaf and to a dewdrop on a blade of grass.

When Gautama came to debate, Mahavira greeted him by naming his secret doubt, whether the soul exists. Gautama had reasoned that the soul cannot be seen like a jar, so it might not exist, like a flower in the sky.
The Kalpa Sutra's translator notes that Indrabhuti Gautama died twelve years after becoming omniscient, having lived fifty years as a monk and ninety-two years in all.
A Jain story book says that once Gautama joined Mahavira, the priest Somil cancelled his great sacrifice at Apapa and set all the animals free.
In a Jain story book, Indrabhuti was angry that Mahavira taught in Ardha-Magadhi, the people's language, instead of Sanskrit. He set out to debate him with his 500 students.
Gautama and his brothers Agnibhuti and Vayubhuti were Vedic scholars who each taught 500 pupils. All three later became ganadharas, chief disciples of Mahavira.
A Jain story book says 4,400 Brahmins came to Somil's sacrifice at Apapa, including eleven famous scholars, and Indrabhuti stood out as the head priest.
On Diwali morning Jain temples offer Nirvan ladoo sweets after prayers to Mahavira. Gautama's omniscience is marked the same day, and the Jain year starts on the day after Diwali.
Jain tradition says Gautama compiled Mahavira's teachings into twelve parts, the Agamas, which were passed on by mouth. Svetambaras and Digambaras later kept different, incomplete versions.

quiz.q: What was Gautama Swami's birth name?
How many chief disciples (ganadharas) did Mahavira have?
Which festival is linked with Gautama's attainment of full knowledge?
quiz.why: Jains link his omniscience with Diwali and the new year.

quiz.q: What do Svetambara Jains write at the new year as a sign of good luck?
options: His name in new account books
quiz.why: Svetambara Jains write Gautama Swami's name in new account books.
